To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Nestlings signal need for food by begging and parents respond to both nestling need and condition, but not to the extent that they should.

(i) Nestlings signal their need for food by increased begging; (ii) parents feed nestlings dependent on both need (i.e., begging) and condition; and (iii) the effect of need and condition on feeding rate depends on parental workload as measured by brood size.
(1) Nestlings increase their begging rate when food is withheld, (2) nestling condition does not affect begging rate, and (3) parents adjust their provisioning rate to the need of their offspring.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of parental care in the barn swallow (Hirundo rusitca) in response to the need for and condition of their offspring.
the question how parents allocate food among their offspring.
the evolution of begging and parental care in the barn swallow.

parents are selected to maximize fitness and therefore allocate care among their offspring in relation to the reproductive value of offspring, and that nestlings have been hypothesised to signal need for care reliably through their behavior, but offspring also condition as reflected by reproductive value may affect begging and hence parental care.
nestlings signal their condition and parents adjust their provisioning accordingly, but this is true only when the nestling's need is not too great.
nestlings signal their needs by begging behavior, and parents adjust their feeding rates to offspring need and condition, but only when they have sufficient time to attend to all offspring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
parents are selected to allocate food among nestlings based on both need and offspring condition and that nestlings signal their condition to parents by their begging behavior.
parents are selected to maximize the fitness of their offspring and that they are able to discriminate among their offspring in relation to both their need for food and their condition.
parents allocate food in relation to offspring need and condition, but the effect of need and condition on parental allocation depends on the workload.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the allocation of parental care is a dynamic and flexible response to a variety of environmental and biological conditions.

nestlings are selected to beg more for food when their need is greater, and parents are selected to feed offspring depending on their need and condition, but these responses may be limited by parental workload.
